summary: This Wikipedia-derived note profiles Jackie Robinson, a second baseman who played ten MLB seasons with the Brooklyn Dodgers from 1947 to 1956. It lists his career statistics, awards and honors, and his Hall of Fame induction. It also explains his historic role as the first African American to play in the modern MLB era, which broke the baseball color line.
one_line: Jackie Robinson was the Brooklyn Dodgers second baseman who broke MLB's color line in 1947 and became a Hall of Famer.
key_facts: Jackie Robinson was born January 31, 1919, in Cairo, Georgia, and died October 24, 1972, in Stamford, Connecticut, aged 53.
Robinson made his MLB debut on April 15, 1947, for the Brooklyn Dodgers, and his last MLB appearance was on October 10, 1956, for the same team.
Robinson's career statistics include a batting average of .311, 137 home runs and 734 runs batted in.
Robinson was a six-time All-Star from 1949 to 1954.
Robinson won the MLB Rookie of the Year Award in 1947, the inaugural year of the award.
Robinson won the National League Most Valuable Player Award in 1949, becoming the first black player so honored.
Robinson won the NL batting title in 1949 and was the NL stolen base leader in 1947 and 1949.
Robinson played in six World Series and contributed to the Dodgers' 1955 World Series championship.
Jersey number 42 is retired by all MLB teams.
Robinson was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1962, receiving 77.5% of the vote on the first ballot.
Robinson was the first African American to play in Major League Baseball in the modern era.
The Brooklyn Dodgers started Robinson at first base on April 15, 1947, breaking the baseball color line.
Robinson's signing heralded the end of racial segregation in professional baseball, which had relegated black players to the Negro leagues since the 1880s.
